lesson.title: From Molarity to Moles: Solution Stoichiometry
lesson.summary: Solution stoichiometry combines molarity with the mole ratios from a balanced equation, letting chemists calculate exactly how much of one dissolved substance is needed to react with, or is produced from, another, using volumes instead of masses.
lesson.body:
Most reactions in a real chemistry lab do not happen between dry solids poured together. They happen in solution, with reactants dissolved in water and measured out by volume using a graduated cylinder, pipette, or burette. Solution stoichiometry is what happens when you take the mole ratio method from ordinary stoichiometry and combine it with molarity, so that instead of starting from a mass in grams, you start from a volume and a concentration.

The bridge is the molarity equation itself: moles equals molarity times volume, or n = M x V. This is exactly the same role that molar mass played when converting grams to moles in solid-based stoichiometry. Once you have moles of one substance, everything else works exactly as before: use the coefficients in the balanced equation to find the mole ratio to whatever substance you actually want, then convert those moles into whatever final unit the question asks for, whether that is grams, moles, or another volume and concentration.

Consider the precipitation reaction between silver nitrate and sodium chloride: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3. Suppose you have 25.0 mL of a 0.400 M NaCl solution and want to know what volume of 0.250 M AgNO3 solution is needed to react with it completely. Start by finding moles of NaCl: convert 25.0 mL to 0.0250 L, then multiply by the molarity, 0.0250 L times 0.400 mol/L, which gives 0.0100 mol NaCl. The balanced equation shows a 1 to 1 mole ratio between NaCl and AgNO3, so 0.0100 mol NaCl requires 0.0100 mol AgNO3. Finally, solve for the volume of AgNO3 solution needed by rearranging the molarity equation to V = n / M: 0.0100 mol divided by 0.250 mol/L equals 0.0400 L, or 40.0 mL.

This volume-to-volume style of calculation, moles in, mole ratio applied, moles out, is the exact backbone of one of the most important techniques in all of quantitative chemistry: titration. In a titration, a solution of precisely known concentration is added, drop by drop, to a solution of unknown concentration, and solution stoichiometry is the tool that turns the volume measured at the end of that process into a concentration you did not know before.
